transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-03-04 UTC 15:30
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ethan Park (Redwood SE), Rina Sato (Redwood CSM), Carlos Ruiz (BrightScale EM), Priya Patel (BrightScale SRE), Liam O'Connor (BrightScale Product)

Summary (auto-gen - may be incomplete): follow-up on last week's reliability incident where customers saw a burst of 5xx/timeouts during a ramp; discuss root cause hypotheses, short-term mitigations (retries/backoff, client changes), and next steps for a deeper debug and ramp tests.

00:00:00 Maya: ok hey everyone, thanks for joining, um we're gonna keep this tight a follow up from last week's incident. quick roll call?
00:00:08 Carlos: carlos here, priya here, and liam yep
00:00:11 Maya: great, thanks. ethan and rina from our side as well, and maya.
00:00:20 Ethan: hi all. i pulled together some initial node metrics and we'll walk through those in a minute.
00:00:26 Priya: thanks, quick note, production went into degraded mode for about 18 minutes last tuesday at 10:12 UTC. we had timeouts from our client, about 2-3% errors turned into 503s, then back to normal.
00:00:38 Maya: yeah that matches what we saw from our telemetry. there was a spike in 5xx errors and increased latencies at the same window.
00:00:48 Liam: curious if this was a model-level OOM or infra thing. our logs show some retries with exponential backoff but still a fair number of failures.
00:00:59 Ethan: initial hypothesis: two possible paths — either the autoscaler overshot and nodes were transiently unhealthy, or there was a short network partition in the region that caused requests to hit fallback paths, leading to queueing on the runtime and 5xx. we also saw increased KD cache ("K-V cash") misses which added CPU overhead. note: transcription might say k-v cash.
00:01:20 Carlos: ok, can you show the metrics?
00:01:24 Ethan: sure, quick screen — node CPU and GPU utilization, queue depths, and per-request tail latencies.
00:01:30 [screen share described: spike in queue depth at 10:10-10:18 UTC, node CPU jitter, one node reported repeated 500s and then finished garbage collection cycles]
00:01:45 Ethan: so you can see here around 10:10 the queue depth increases sharply. tail latency hits 2.1s from a baseline of ~300ms. we had one worker node that reported repeated 500s while it was under high swap activity — suspected memory pressure.
00:02:02 Priya: memory pressure — is that model KV cache growth or something else? our model bundle hasn't changed.
00:02:10 Ethan: most likely lock contention on the KV cache when a new prefix load happened; the runtime serializes some parts during cache population which can block other requests briefly. plus we saw a handful of OOM warnings on system logs.
00:02:22 Rina: just to add, the incident coincided with a customer-side batch job that ramped traffic by ~3x for a short window — Carlos, is that expected?
00:02:30 Carlos: yes, we had an internal reindex job that created a traffic burst, we should have communicated it but it was missed.
00:02:36 Liam: that explains it then, so it's a load pattern problem plus runtime behavior under sudden ramps. what about rate limits? were there any 429s?
00:02:45 Ethan: interestingly, we did not see 429s centrally — requests were being accepted but then dropped with 5xx, suggesting the service accepted them then failed internally.
00:02:55 Maya: ok so short-term mitigations — client retry/backoff, and maybe configure a circuit breaker on certain endpoints to fail-fast rather than pile up.
00:03:05 Priya: we already have retries but our retry window is tight — we're doing 3 quick retries with small jitter. during the incident that led to cascading failures.
00:03:14 Ethan: recommendation: widen backoff, add jitter, and optionally detect early 5xx spikes to fail fast for a short TTL on the client side. we can share a suggested backoff config.
00:03:26 Maya: also from Redwood side we can enable a short-term safety throttle on your project to limit concurrency to a predictable level while you run controlled ramps. that avoids uncontrolled queueing across many clients.
00:03:38 Carlos: what's the cost or impact on latency for safety throttle?
00:03:42 Rina: it will increase tail latency for some requests if we queue them client-side, but reduces failure rate overall. think of it as shaping. for the pilot we can make it conservative.
00:03:53 Priya: ok, next — logs. we need the request IDs that failed so we can correlate them with our traces.
00:03:58 Ethan: yes we've collected the request IDs for the spike window; we'll upload them to the shared folder. they include node IDs and timestamps.
00:04:10 [brief cross talk — someone drops a link for shared drive]
00:04:18 Maya: i'll log an action item to share the logs and timeline — ethan will take the lead.
00:04:24 Carlos: thanks. long term, should we consider a dedicated pool? we saw that burst from other internal jobs could impact the pilot.
00:04:31 Maya: yes, Dedicated GPU pool gives isolation and predictable throughput. for the POC we can propose a small dedicated pool with burst capacity; we also discussed autoscale tuning to avoid thrashing.
00:04:44 Liam: curious on the autoscaler behaviour — did it spin up new nodes during the window and those nodes were unhealthy during warmup?
00:04:52 Ethan: we saw scaling events just before the spike, but the main issue seems to be many requests arriving while the new nodes were still initializing their KV cache and warmup, causing higher latencies and some 5xx from timeouts in the warmup code path.
00:05:07 Priya: is there a warmup hook we can call from the client to pre-load prefixes?
00:05:13 Ethan: good question — we have an API to pre-warm common prefixes, but it requires a separate job to push those prefixes; we can share the doc and a script. this reduces the cold path on first request.
00:05:25 Carlos: that'd help. we'll plan to run a warmup job before heavy windows.
00:05:29 Rina: also, we noticed some malformed requests from the customer's side that triggered additional validation overhead — not the main cause, but worth cleaning up.
00:05:38 Liam: noted.
00:05:42 Ethan: quick note on rate limiting: although you didn't hit 429s, we do have service-level concurrent request limits; if many clients overwhelm the runtime, the system accepts requests and then might return 5xx if the runtime internal queue is saturated. so client-side throttles are still important.
00:05:58 Maya: ok let's capture concrete next steps and who owns them.
00:06:03 [discussion — reiterating action items and owners, see action_items field]
00:06:20 Carlos: can we also get a proposed short-term retry/backoff config from Redwood? we can patch our clients quickly.
00:06:26 Ethan: yes i'll propose something — e.g., initial backoff 250ms, multiply by 2 with jitter, up to 8s, max 5 retries, and add detection to short-circuit on sustained 5xx spikes for 30s. we'll test locally and share the patch.
00:06:44 Priya: that sounds reasonable. we'll test with the ramp.
00:06:48 Liam: anything on observability? can we get per-request traces and a view of tail latencies by prefix?
00:06:54 Rina: we can share per-route dashboards and enable additional retention for the project temporarily; that will help you triage.
00:07:03 Carlos: excellent. also curious about SLA and incident reporting — we saw the degraded period but didn't get an automated alert from Redwood.
00:07:12 Maya: yes, apologies — our alerting threshold missed the short tail spike due to conservative thresholds. we're going to adjust thresholds for pilot customers and enable a Canary alert for 5xx rate >0.5% over 5 minutes.
00:07:25 Priya: please also add a contact escalation path; we called support but the ticket was delayed.
00:07:30 Maya: noted — i'll follow up with our support manager to make sure the escalation contact is in place for your account.
00:07:37 [short pause, background noise, someone says "sorry, dog barking"]
00:07:45 Ethan: technical question from me — can BrightScale share the exact request size distribution during the spike? it will help us reproduce.
00:07:53 Carlos: yes, we'll include that in the load script.
00:07:57 Ethan: perfect. my plan after this call: gather the node logs, compile a timeline, run a synthetic replay against a staging cluster with the same load, and propose a patch (backoff + server throttle) we can try in production.
00:08:12 Priya: and we'll run the controlled ramp and run the warmup script in staging first, then schedule production rollout.
00:08:18 Maya: ok any final questions?
00:08:22 Liam: one small item — can you also confirm if KV cache population is single-threaded per model? that would inform our warmup parallelism.
00:08:30 Ethan: it's mostly single-threaded for the critical path but there are async parts; we'll document exact behavior.
00:08:37 Carlos: thanks everyone.
00:08:39 Maya: great, thanks, i'll send the notes and action items. we'll reconvene next week same time unless we schedule the deep dive sooner.
00:08:47 Rina: thanks all.
00:08:50 [meeting ends]

Notes on transcription: speaker labels are approximate, there are occasional mis-hearings (e.g., "KV cache" transcribed as "K-V cash"), and some timestamps are coarse. The transcript focuses on reliability incident root cause hypotheses: autoscaler warmup + KV cache population + memory pressure leading to 5xx; short-term mitigations: client retry/backoff, circuit breaker, temporary safety throttle, dedicated pool consideration; next steps include log sharing, controlled ramp, warmup scripts, and a SE-led deep dive.
